persona.name: Prakash Reddy
persona.background: He runs a small retail business and spends most of the day seated at the shop counter, with occasional heavy lifting during stock deliveries. He has been avoiding exertion recently because of episodes of dizziness and breathlessness.

diagnoses.name: Severe aortic stenosis
diagnoses.description: Harsh/rough diamond-shaped ejection mid-systolic murmur best heard at the base with radiation to neck; parvus and tardus pulse with apicocarotid delay; severe AS may have soft A2 and reduced systolic/pulse pressures.

diagnoses.name: Chronic stable angina pectoris
diagnoses.description: Constricting chest discomfort brought on by exertion/emotion and relieved within minutes by rest or sublingual glyceryl trinitrate; typical episodes last 2–5 minutes.

diagnoses.name: Acute coronary syndrome (myocardial infarction/unstable angina)
diagnoses.description: Severe chest pain lasting >20 minutes that typically does not respond to sublingual GTN; may be associated with breathlessness, nausea/vomiting, diaphoresis, collapse/syncope.

diagnoses.name: Acute pericarditis
diagnoses.description: Sharp substernal pleuritic chest pain that may be relieved by sitting up and leaning forward; ECG classically shows diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression.

diagnoses.name: Pulmonary arterial hypertension
diagnoses.description: Insidious exertional dyspnea with signs such as loud P2, narrow splitting of S2, pulmonary ejection sound/murmur, and may have prominent V wave if tricuspid regurgitation is present; echo is useful for detection.

diagnoses.name: Tricuspid regurgitation
diagnoses.description: Blowing pansystolic murmur at the lower-left sternal border that increases during inspiration (De Carvallo’s sign) with raised JVP and giant v waves (cv wave).

diagnoses.name: Constrictive pericarditis
diagnoses.description: Raised JVP with prominent X and Y descents; Kussmaul’s sign often present; pericardial knock may occur in early diastole; imaging may show pericardial thickening.

diagnoses.name: Myocarditis (acute myocarditis)
diagnoses.description: May present with heart failure, acute myocardial infarction-like presentation or sudden death; exam may show soft muffled heart sounds, prominent S3, inappropriate tachycardia, arrhythmias/conduction blocks; troponin/CK may be raised and echo may show global hypokinesia.

diagnoses.name: Dilated cardiomyopathy
diagnoses.description: Dilated ventricular chambers with systolic dysfunction; can cause chronic heart failure and functional mitral/tricuspid regurgitation due to annular dilatation.

diagnoses.name: Infective endocarditis
diagnoses.description: Features include evidence of new regurgitant murmur (a new diastolic murmur is a diagnostic feature), embolic manifestations (petechiae, splinter hemorrhages, Janeway lesions), and immunological phenomena (Osler nodes, Roth spots); blood cultures are crucial.

initialComplaint: For the last few months I get tightness in the chest when I walk fast or carry boxes, and twice I felt like I would faint. Lately I also get breathless on exertion.
medicalHistory: No documented cardiac diagnosis. No known prior rheumatic fever mentioned. No prior hospitalizations reported. Medication history not provided.

redHerrings: Chest pain on exertion could suggest chronic stable angina pectoris. Breathlessness could suggest pulmonary arterial hypertension or dilated cardiomyopathy. Near-syncope could also occur with arrhythmias seen in myocarditis. A systolic murmur could be confused with mitral regurgitation unless the ejection (mid-systolic) quality, stopping before A2, and the parvus-tardus carotid pulse are elicited.

precomputedExplanations.description: **Severe aortic stenosis** is a critical narrowing of the aortic valve causing fixed obstruction to left ventricular outflow. This leads to pressure overload, reduced ability to augment cardiac output during exertion, and can progress to **syncope**, **angina**, and **heart failure** symptoms.
keySymptoms: **Exertional chest tightness (angina)** - Fixed outflow obstruction increases LV oxygen demand and limits supply during exertion.
**Exertional near-syncope/syncope** - Inability to raise cardiac output with exercise causes cerebral hypoperfusion and faintness.
**Progressive exertional dyspnea** - Elevated LV filling pressures from pressure overload lead to pulmonary congestion on exertion.
**Parvus et tardus pulse** - Slow-rising, low-volume carotid upstroke reflects severe obstruction across the aortic valve.
**Apicocarotid delay** - Delayed carotid upstroke relative to apex indicates prolonged LV ejection in aortic stenosis.
**Low systolic and pulse pressure** - Reduced stroke volume from fixed obstruction produces “systolic decapitation” and narrow pulse pressure.
**Heaving (thrusting) apex beat** - Concentric LV hypertrophy from pressure overload creates a sustained, forceful apical impulse.
**Harsh ejection mid-systolic murmur radiating to carotids** - Classic crescendo–decrescendo murmur from turbulent flow across stenotic valve.
**Late-peaking systolic murmur** - Later peak correlates with more severe stenosis due to prolonged ejection time.
**Soft/absent A2 or paradoxical split S2** - Severely restricted valve closure and delayed LV ejection alter the second heart sound.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: The patient has the classic symptomatic triad of **severe aortic stenosis**: exertional **angina**, exertional **syncope/near-syncope**, and progressive exertional **dyspnea** suggesting developing heart failure. Examination strongly supports AS with **parvus et tardus** and **apicocarotid delay**, a **heaving LV apex**, and a harsh **ejection mid-systolic** murmur maximal at the aortic area with radiation to the **carotids** and **late peaking**. The **soft/single A2** and possible **paradoxical split S2** further indicate severe obstruction. This pattern differs from **mitral regurgitation**, which typically has an apical **pan-systolic** murmur continuing to **A2** and a brisk, high-volume pulse.

precomputedExplanations.description: **Chronic stable angina pectoris** is predictable, exertion-related chest discomfort due to fixed **coronary artery** stenosis causing transient myocardial ischemia. Symptoms are typically relieved by rest or nitrates and are not primarily explained by valvular outflow obstruction.
keySymptoms: **Exertional chest tightness** - Constricting substernal discomfort triggered by exertion and relieved within minutes of rest.
**Predictable threshold** - Similar workload reliably provokes symptoms, reflecting stable fixed coronary supply-demand mismatch.
**Radiation** - Pain may radiate to left arm, neck, jaw, or epigastrium during exertion.
**Autonomic symptoms** - Diaphoresis or nausea can accompany ischemic discomfort, especially with higher intensity exertion.
**Normal between episodes** - Patients are often asymptomatic at rest with no ongoing chest pain.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: This patient’s exertional chest tightness could superficially resemble **stable angina**, because it is brought on by exertion and relieved by rest. However, the presence of exertional **near-syncope/syncope** and progressive exertional **dyspnea** strongly suggests a hemodynamic outflow limitation rather than isolated coronary ischemia. The examination findings—**parvus et tardus** pulse with **apicocarotid delay**, low systolic/pulse pressure, and a harsh **ejection mid-systolic** murmur radiating to the carotids with soft/single **A2**—are classic for **severe aortic stenosis**. Therefore, labeling this as chronic stable angina misses the primary valvular cause and the high-risk implications.
precomputedExplanations.whyIncorrectForCase: While exertional chest discomfort can occur in both conditions, this patient has hallmark signs of **severe aortic stenosis** (parvus et tardus, carotid radiation, ejection murmur, soft **A2**). Exertional syncope and the specific pulse/murmur characteristics are not explained by uncomplicated **chronic stable angina**.
keyDifferencesFromCorrect: **Primary mechanism** - Stable angina is **coronary ischemia** from fixed plaque; severe AS is **LV outflow obstruction** from a stenotic aortic valve.
**Syncope on exertion** - Uncommon in stable angina; classic high-risk symptom in **severe aortic stenosis** due to fixed cardiac output.
**Carotid pulse** - Stable angina usually has normal upstroke; severe AS shows **slow-rising, low-volume (parvus et tardus)** pulse.
**Murmur timing/quality** - Stable angina has no defining murmur; severe AS has harsh **crescendo-decrescendo ejection** murmur that stops before **A2**.
**Second heart sound** - Stable angina does not cause a soft/single **A2**; severe AS often has diminished **A2** and may show paradoxical split.
**Post-VPC response** - Not a feature of stable angina; severe AS murmur intensity **increases post-VPC** (per bedside hemodynamics).
missingFindings: **Ischemic ECG changes during pain** - Lack of exertional ST depression/T-wave inversion evidence weakens isolated stable angina diagnosis.
**Coronary risk-pattern symptom profile** - Absence of typical radiation/autonomic ischemic features makes pure angina less compelling here.
**No valvular signs expected** - Stable angina should not produce **parvus et tardus**, **apicocarotid delay**, or carotid-radiating ejection murmur.
**No characteristic S2 change** - Stable angina would not explain soft/single **A2** or paradoxical splitting seen in severe AS.

precomputedExplanations.description: **Acute coronary syndrome (ACS)** is myocardial ischemia from acute plaque rupture and coronary thrombosis, presenting as **unstable angina** or **myocardial infarction**. It typically causes new, worsening, or rest chest pain and may show **ECG changes** and/or **troponin elevation**.
keySymptoms: **Chest pain at rest** - Prolonged pressure-like pain occurring without exertion, often lasting over 20 minutes.
**Crescendo angina** - Rapidly worsening frequency, severity, or duration of angina over days to weeks.
**Autonomic symptoms** - Diaphoresis, nausea, and anxiety accompanying ischemic discomfort from sympathetic activation.
**Radiation of pain** - Discomfort may radiate to left arm, jaw, neck, or back with ischemia.
**Dyspnea** - Shortness of breath can be an anginal equivalent, especially in older adults.
**Syncope** - Can occur with arrhythmias or hemodynamic compromise during acute ischemic events.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: This patient has exertional chest tightness relieved by rest, which can resemble angina; however, the overall syndrome is dominated by classic signs of **severe aortic stenosis**. The presence of **parvus et tardus** pulse with **apicocarotid delay**, a **harsh ejection mid-systolic crescendo–decrescendo murmur** radiating to the carotids, and a **soft/single A2** strongly indicates fixed LV outflow obstruction rather than acute coronary plaque rupture. His exertional near-syncope and progressive exertional dyspnea form the typical symptomatic triad of severe AS (angina, syncope, dyspnea/heart failure). ACS would be expected to present with acute instability (rest pain, dynamic ECG changes, biomarkers) rather than a months-long exertional pattern with classic valvular findings.
precomputedExplanations.whyIncorrectForCase: The presentation is chronic and exertional with relief at rest, not the acute/rest or rapidly progressive pattern typical of **ACS**. The examination findings (ejection murmur to carotids, **parvus et tardus**, soft **A2**) point to **severe aortic stenosis**, not coronary thrombosis.
keyDifferencesFromCorrect: **Murmur timing/quality** - ACS has no specific systolic ejection murmur; severe AS has **harsh ejection mid-systolic** murmur stopping before **A2**.
**Carotid pulse** - ACS usually has normal pulse contour; severe AS shows **slow-rising, low-volume (parvus et tardus)** pulse.
**Second heart sound (A2)** - ACS does not cause a soft/absent **A2**; severe AS often has **soft/single A2** and may have paradoxical split.
**Syncope mechanism** - ACS syncope is often arrhythmic/ischemic; severe AS syncope is exertional from fixed outflow obstruction and inability to augment cardiac output.
**Course** - ACS is acute (hours–days) with instability; severe AS progresses over months/years with exertional symptoms.
**Post-VPC murmur response** - ACS has no characteristic post-VPC murmur change; severe AS murmur **increases after VPC** (post-extrasystolic potentiation).
missingFindings: **Rest or prolonged chest pain** - Absence of persistent/rest pain makes unstable angina or MI less likely here.
**Dynamic ECG changes** - No reported ST-segment/T-wave changes that would support acute ischemia.
**Troponin elevation** - No biomarker evidence of myocardial necrosis provided for MI diagnosis.
**New acute hemodynamic instability** - No acute hypotension, shock, or sudden pulmonary edema described.
**Typical ACS symptom cluster** - No diaphoresis, nausea/vomiting, or acute distress temporally linked to pain episodes.

precomputedExplanations.description: **Acute pericarditis** is inflammation of the pericardial sac, most often viral/idiopathic, causing sharp pleuritic chest pain and a characteristic pericardial friction rub. It can produce ECG changes (diffuse ST elevation/PR depression) and may be complicated by **pericardial effusion** or **tamponade**.
keySymptoms: **Sharp pleuritic chest pain** - Worse with inspiration/coughing; typically improves when sitting forward, unlike exertional angina.
**Positional chest pain relief** - Pain classically decreases leaning forward and increases when supine due to pericardial irritation.
**Pericardial friction rub** - Scratchy, triphasic sound best at left sternal border; may vary with posture/respiration.
**Fever/viral prodrome** - Low-grade fever, myalgias, and recent infection commonly precede idiopathic/viral pericarditis.
**Dyspnea** - Usually from pain-limited breathing or effusion; not classically exertional progressive breathlessness.
**ECG diffuse ST elevation** - Widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression supports inflammatory pericardial disease.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: This patient’s symptoms are dominated by **exertional chest tightness relieved by rest**, exertional **near-syncope**, and progressive **exertional dyspnea**, which strongly suggests a fixed outflow obstruction syndrome. Examination findings of **parvus et tardus** pulse, **apicocarotid delay**, low pulse pressure, and a harsh **ejection mid-systolic crescendo–decrescendo murmur** radiating to the carotids with soft/absent **A2** are classic for **severe aortic stenosis**. Acute pericarditis typically causes pleuritic, positional chest pain with a **friction rub** and supportive ECG changes rather than a carotid-radiating systolic ejection murmur and slow-rising pulse.
precomputedExplanations.whyIncorrectForCase: The chest discomfort described is **effort-related and relieved by rest**, not **pleuritic/positional**, making **acute pericarditis** unlikely. The physical findings (parvus et tardus, carotid radiation, ejection systolic murmur with late peaking, soft **A2**) point to **severe aortic stenosis**, not pericardial inflammation.
keyDifferencesFromCorrect: **Chest pain quality** - Pericarditis is sharp/pleuritic and positional; **severe aortic stenosis** causes exertional pressure/tightness (angina).
**Trigger/relief pattern** - Pericarditis pain worsens with inspiration/supine and improves leaning forward; **severe aortic stenosis** pain is provoked by exertion and relieved by rest.
**Auscultation hallmark** - Pericarditis has a **pericardial friction rub**; **severe aortic stenosis** has a harsh **ejection systolic** murmur radiating to carotids.
**Pulse character** - Pericarditis does not cause **parvus et tardus**; **severe aortic stenosis** produces slow-rising, low-volume carotid upstroke with apicocarotid delay.
**Syncope mechanism** - Pericarditis rarely causes exertional syncope; **severe aortic stenosis** commonly causes exertional presyncope/syncope from fixed cardiac output.
**ECG pattern** - Pericarditis shows diffuse ST elevation/PR depression; **severe aortic stenosis** more often shows LVH/strain or may be nonspecific.
missingFindings: **Pleuritic, positional chest pain** - Absence of pain worsened by inspiration/supine argues strongly against pericarditis.
**Pericardial friction rub** - No rub described; its presence is a key bedside clue for pericarditis.
**Diffuse ST elevation with PR depression** - No ECG features provided to support pericardial inflammation.
**Fever or recent viral illness** - No systemic inflammatory/viral prodrome symptoms are reported.
**Pericardial effusion/tamponade signs** - No raised JVP, muffled heart sounds, or pulsus paradoxus to suggest significant effusion.

precomputedExplanations.description: **Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH)** is a progressive disorder with elevated pulmonary arterial pressure due to pulmonary arteriolar remodeling, causing increased right ventricular afterload. It typically leads to exertional dyspnea, fatigue, chest pain, and syncope from inability to augment cardiac output during exercise.
keySymptoms: **Exertional dyspnea** - Breathlessness on activity from limited pulmonary vascular reserve and reduced forward flow.
**Exertional syncope/presyncope** - Near-fainting during exertion due to fixed cardiac output and RV failure physiology.
**Chest pain** - Substernal pressure from RV ischemia or pulmonary artery stretch during exertion.
**Fatigue** - Low effective cardiac output and impaired oxygen delivery during activity.
**Peripheral edema** - Late sign from right heart failure with systemic venous congestion and fluid retention.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: This patient has exertional dyspnea and exertional presyncope, which can occur in **PAH**. However, the dominant findings are classic for **severe aortic stenosis**: **parvus et tardus** pulse with **apicocarotid delay**, low systolic/pulse pressure, and a harsh **ejection mid-systolic crescendo–decrescendo murmur** at the **aortic area** radiating to the **carotids**. These point to a fixed left ventricular outflow obstruction rather than pulmonary vascular disease. The murmur timing (ends before **A2**) and late peaking further support severe **AS**, not PAH.
precomputedExplanations.whyIncorrectForCase: PAH does not explain the hallmark peripheral pulse abnormality (**parvus et tardus**) and **apicocarotid delay**, which indicate left-sided outflow obstruction. The auscultatory pattern described (base **ejection** murmur radiating to neck with soft/single **A2**) is characteristic of **severe aortic stenosis**, not PAH.
keyDifferencesFromCorrect: **Primary pathology** - PAH is pulmonary arteriolar disease causing RV pressure overload; **severe AS** is valvular LV outflow obstruction.
**Pulse character** - PAH usually has a normal carotid upstroke; **severe AS** causes **slow-rising, low-volume (parvus et tardus)** carotid pulse.
**Murmur location** - PAH may have a **tricuspid regurgitation** murmur at left lower sternal border; **severe AS** has a harsh **ejection systolic** murmur at **aortic area** radiating to carotids.
**Second heart sound** - PAH classically has loud **P2**; **severe AS** often has soft/absent **A2** and may have paradoxical split.
**Ventricular findings** - PAH produces RV heave and right-sided signs; **severe AS** produces a heaving LV apex and possible **S4**.
missingFindings: **Accentuated P2** - Expected in PAH from high pulmonary artery pressure; not described here.
**Right ventricular heave** - PAH typically causes a parasternal lift from RV hypertrophy; not reported.
**Tricuspid regurgitation murmur** - Common in advanced PAH at left lower sternal border; absent in this case description.
**Raised JVP and peripheral edema** - Support right heart failure in PAH; not mentioned despite months of symptoms.
**Clear evidence of pulmonary etiology** - PAH often has hypoxemia, lung disease signs, or connective tissue history; none provided.

precomputedExplanations.description: **Tricuspid regurgitation (TR)** is systolic backflow of blood from the right ventricle into the right atrium due to tricuspid valve incompetence. It is most commonly functional from right ventricular dilation (e.g., pulmonary hypertension) and typically produces right-sided heart failure manifestations.
keySymptoms: **Fatigue** - Reduced forward cardiac output and systemic venous congestion can cause low energy and weakness.
**Peripheral edema** - Systemic venous hypertension leads to ankle swelling that worsens later in the day.
**Abdominal distension/ascites** - Venous congestion causes fluid accumulation in the peritoneal cavity and bloating.
**Right upper quadrant discomfort** - Congestive hepatomegaly stretches the liver capsule causing aching pain.
**Pulsatile neck veins** - Prominent **JVP** with systolic **v-waves** reflects regurgitant flow into right atrium.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: This patient’s presentation is dominated by exertional **angina**, exertional **near-syncope/syncope**, and progressive exertional **dyspnea**, which is the classic symptomatic triad of severe **aortic stenosis**. The examination described—**parvus et tardus** pulse with **apicocarotid delay**, low pulse pressure, and a harsh **ejection mid-systolic crescendo–decrescendo murmur** radiating to the carotids with soft/single **A2**—strongly localizes pathology to the aortic valve outflow. In contrast, **tricuspid regurgitation** produces a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration and is associated with systemic venous congestion signs rather than carotid-radiating ejection murmurs.
precomputedExplanations.whyIncorrectForCase: The case lacks right-sided congestion features typical of **TR** (e.g., raised **JVP**, hepatomegaly, ascites, peripheral edema). The murmur and pulse findings are classic for severe **aortic stenosis**, not a right-sided holosystolic regurgitant lesion.
keyDifferencesFromCorrect: **Murmur timing/shape** - **TR** is **pan-systolic/holosystolic**; severe **aortic stenosis** is **ejection mid-systolic** (crescendo–decrescendo) and ends before **A2**.
**Murmur location** - **TR** is loudest at **left lower sternal border**; severe **aortic stenosis** is loudest at **aortic area** with radiation to **carotids**.
**Respiratory variation** - **TR** increases with **inspiration** (Carvallo sign); severe **aortic stenosis** does not characteristically increase with inspiration.
**Pulse character** - **TR** does not cause **parvus et tardus**; severe **aortic stenosis** causes **slow-rising, low-volume** carotid pulse with **apicocarotid delay**.
**Second heart sound** - **TR** does not typically cause soft/single **A2**; severe **aortic stenosis** may have **soft/absent A2** and **paradoxical splitting**.
**Symptom pattern** - **TR** causes systemic venous congestion symptoms; severe **aortic stenosis** causes exertional **angina**, **syncope**, and **dyspnea**.
missingFindings: **Raised JVP with prominent v-waves** - Expected in significant **TR**; absence argues against right atrial systolic reflux.
**Pansystolic murmur at LLSB increasing with inspiration** - Hallmark auscultatory feature of **TR**; not described here.
**Pulsatile hepatomegaly** - Suggests severe **TR** with hepatic venous systolic flow reversal; not reported.
**Peripheral edema/ascites** - Typical of right-sided heart failure from **TR**; not present in the case.
**Right ventricular heave** - Would support right-sided volume overload; exam instead suggests **LV** pressure overload (heaving apex).

differentialDiagnoses.name: Mitral regurgitation
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: Differentiate by murmur site and character: MR is pansystolic at apex continuing till A2; AS is ejection mid-systolic at aortic area + apex and stops before A2. Also use post-VPC intensity and carotid pulse contour: AS increases post-VPC and has slow-rising low-volume pulse; MR shows no change/decrease post-VPC with quick-rising high-volume pulse.
differentialDiagnoses.textbookReference: “Aortic stenosis… Usually ejection-mid systolic. Stops before A2… Post-VPC intensity increases… Carotid pulse slow rising, low volume.”

differentialDiagnoses.name: Aortic regurgitation (coexistent or alternative lesion)
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: Look for AR pulse features and peripheral signs: AR has bounding/collapsing pulse and wide pulse pressure; AS typically has low systolic and pulse pressures and parvus et tardus/anacrotic pulse (severe). Consider pulsus bisferiens when AS is associated with AR.
differentialDiagnoses.textbookReference: “Peripheral pulses… bounding, or collapsing… increased/wide pulse pressure” and “Pulse: Parvus and tardus… Pulsus bisferiens if AS is associated aortic regurgitation (AR).”

differentialDiagnoses.name: Aortic sclerosis
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: Aortic sclerosis produces a systolic ejection murmur but without significant aortic obstruction; pulse and BP are normal, and it is typically asymptomatic.
differentialDiagnoses.textbookReference: “Aortic sclerosis… may produce a systolic ejection murmur without any symptoms. Pulse and BP will be normal.”

idealPathway.diagnosticApproach: Systematically confirm symptomatic aortic stenosis by (1) targeted history for the symptomatic triad (dyspnea, angina, syncope) and exercise intolerance; (2) focused cardiovascular examination emphasizing severe AS signs (anacrotic/parvus et tardus pulse, apico-carotid delay, late-peaking ejection mid-systolic murmur radiating to neck, paradoxical split S2, S4); (3) cost-effective investigations starting with ECG and chest X-ray, then definitive echocardiography with Doppler to evaluate severity/gradient and associated AR; and (4) differentiate from similar systolic murmurs (especially mitral regurgitation) using murmur timing/site, post-VPC intensity change, and carotid pulse characteristics, and consider aortic sclerosis when murmur occurs with normal pulse/BP and no symptoms.
